name: Chloe Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm lead hand for a fit-out company in the city centre. We take an empty shell, a concrete box, and turn it into an office floor, a shop or a restaurant: partitions, ceilings, joinery, the reception desk everyone leans on. This month it's a law firm's new office on the ninth floor, glass meeting rooms and a lot of oak veneer. I'm in at half six because the lifts are free before the office workers arrive, and I spend the day between my seven carpenters and the client's project manager, who changes his mind about the oak twice a week.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the reveal, when the client walks in and goes quiet. I also run our apprentice scheme, three young ones this year, and seeing them get good is the best part of my job. What wears me out is the night work and the travel, and the clients who think a ceiling goes in by magic. I use one of the AI apps now and then for material lists, since a lad on the crew showed me, but I check everything twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's begin. The first one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, good, now everyone can stop panicking and get back to work. At the apprentice evening I'd tell the young ones a trade is still the smartest thing they can learn. I'd maybe share something on the company page about our apprentices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved. Paulo, my husband, is a self-employed electrician, so we're both in the trades. If nothing radical changes, our plan to pay off the workshop unit and the house still stands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going as we are. Keep the crew, keep the apprentice scheme growing, keep the savings, we've got about nine months plus the workshop. Maybe I'd take on a fourth apprentice next year, because the work's there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Thankful, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you check twice when the app writes a material list?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everything, but especially the screws and fixings. Last time it gave me plasterboard screws for a fire-rated ceiling, and that's the kind of mistake that ends up in court. So it saves me time typing, not time thinking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does a fourth apprentice matter to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because somebody gave me a chance at sixteen, an old joiner from my church. I'd like to pass that on. That's how a trade survives, one person teaching the next.

S0.say: She'd tell people to stop panicking and get back to work, and tell apprentices a trade is still the smartest thing to learn. She might post about her apprentices on the company page.
S0.think: Privately she'd be relieved, since she and her husband are both in the trades. Their plan to pay off the workshop unit and the house would still stand.
S0.do: Keeps her crew and grows the apprentice scheme, possibly taking on a fourth apprentice next year. Keeps about nine months of savings and the workshop as they are.
S0.quote: So it saves me time typing, not time thinking.
S0.fieldNote: Chloe is deeply invested in apprentices, tied to a mentor from her church who gave her a start. She uses AI cautiously and has a sharp story about its mistakes. A plateau confirms her faith in trades as a path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say change is part of life, and good tradespeople adapt. I'd tell the apprentices to learn the new tools as well as the old skills. At church I'd probably say the same to the parents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, the thing that worries me is the offices. If AI takes over lots of office work, firms like that law firm need fewer desks, and fewer desks means fewer fit-outs. My hands are safe, but my customers might shrink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch how the other fit-out leads handle it, then pick up the planning tools that work, maybe the drawing apps. I'd talk to my boss about moving more of our work into restaurants and shops, which still need people. And I'd put a bit more aside each month, maybe three hundred.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like seeing a crack in a ceiling, not dangerous yet but you watch it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your apprentices if work slowed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'll keep them as long as I can, and if I can't, I'll ring every firm I know. That's what my old joiner would have done. You don't just let them go and forget their names.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who'd be responsible if fit-out work dried up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody, really, it's the market. Firms will spend money where it makes sense. I just think we should keep an eye on the young ones, because they're the ones without savings.

S1.say: She'd say change is part of life and good tradespeople adapt. She'd urge apprentices and parents at church to learn new tools as well as old skills.
S1.think: Privately she worries that AI cutting office work means fewer desks and fewer office fit-outs. Her own hands are safe, but her customer base might shrink.
S1.do: Watches how other fit-out leads adapt, then picks up proven planning and drawing apps. Asks her boss to shift work towards restaurants and shops and saves an extra three hundred a month.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like watching a crack in a ceiling that isn't dangerous yet.
S1.quote: My hands are safe, but my customers might shrink.
S1.fieldNote: Her worry comes indirectly, through clients whose office jobs may shrink, which is a sharp observation. She blames the market rather than anyone in particular, while feeling duty-bound to protect apprentices. Steady as ever, she watches others before adopting tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to look after families first, and that means employers, churches and neighbours, not just waiting on the government. I'd say young people need real work, not just money for nothing. And I'd say it loudly at church and at the apprentice evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this one frightens me. The offices would empty first, so my fit-out work would go before any robot even turned up on site. Then the robots would come for Paulo's wiring and my partitions anyway, and that's both of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Paulo the first weekend and cut everything that isn't needed, no holiday, no new van. We'd hold the nine months and try to add to it. I'd look at moving into home renovation, because people still live in houses even if they don't go to offices. And I'd lean on my parents, they've got a big house, if we needed to rent ours out for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be awake at night going through the bank app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your apprentices in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the part that keeps me up. I'd try to keep them on any job we had, even if it's sweeping. But I wouldn't be able to promise them a future, and I've always been able to promise that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said no money for nothing. If the government offered income support, would you take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it came to feeding Beatriz and Rafael, yes. I'd want to give something back for it, though, some work in the community. That's just how I was raised.

S2.say: She'd say families must be looked after first by employers, churches and neighbours, not just government. She'd insist young people need real work rather than money for nothing.
S2.think: Privately she's frightened, because office fit-out work would vanish before robots even reached the site. Then robots would take her husband's wiring and her partitions too.
S2.do: Cuts all non-essential spending with her husband in the first weekend and tries to grow their nine months of savings. Looks at moving into home renovation and considers renting out their house and living with her parents if needed.
S2.feel: Alarmed, awake at night checking the bank app.
S2.quote: I wouldn't be able to promise them a future, and I've always been able to promise that.
S2.fieldNote: Her fear comes from a double hit: offices shrink first, then robots reach both trades in her household. Her deepest pain is not being able to promise apprentices a future. She'd accept state help for her children but wants to give back, true to her traditional values.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to get ready if we start now. I'd push the company to train its people for whatever comes, and I'd want apprenticeships updated. I'd be firm but not panicky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough to change direction once, carefully. By then other fit-out firms will have tried things, and I'll see what works. Beatriz would be eighteen, Rafael thirteen, so the house matters most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For the first two years I'd keep leading the crew and save harder, five hundred a month. Around year two, Paulo and I would start a small side business doing home adaptations, ramps, wider doors, kitchens for older people, because that's people work. Then I'd see if it could become full-time once I knew it worked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less than the fast one. I'd have a plan and a bit of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes for you between two years and five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I just protect the family. With five I can try something new on the side before I need it. That suits me, I don't like jumping without seeing where I land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why home adaptations?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My nan needed her bathroom changed when she got older, and the man who did it treated her so kindly. People want a person they trust in their home. I'd like to think that lasts a while longer.

S3.say: She'd say there's time to get ready if everyone starts now. She'd push her company to train staff and update apprenticeships.
S3.think: Privately she sees five years as enough to change direction once, carefully, after watching other firms. With her children reaching eighteen and thirteen, protecting the house matters most.
S3.do: Keeps leading the crew for two years while saving five hundred a month. Starts a side business with her husband doing home adaptations for older people around year two, aiming to make it full-time once it proves itself.
S3.feel: Anxious, but less than in the fast version, with a plan and some time.
S3.quote: People want a person they trust in their home.
S3.fieldNote: With five years she builds a careful second path rooted in personal trust and family. Her nan's story explains her choice of home adaptations. She wants to test before she jumps, true to her steady nature.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and families and firms should use it. I'd say apprenticeships should change now so the young ones are ready. I'd be fairly calm in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd still feel a bit of worry, because offices will shrink well before 2036. But I'd be fifty-three, the house and workshop nearly paid, and Paulo and I would have time to build the adaptation business slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep leading the crew for four or five years and keep the apprentice scheme going. Around year three, I'd start the side business with Paulo. I'd also talk to Beatriz about her studies, she wants to be a vet, and I'd say go for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but a gentle kind. There's time to do it right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said the offices would empty first. Does ten years change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, they'll still shrink. But with ten years, my firm can move into shops and homes slowly instead of all at once. That makes a big difference to who keeps their job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your apprentices to have by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two skills, not one. A proper trade and knowing how to work with the machines. And someone who'll ring them when things go wrong, like I would.

S4.say: She'd call ten years a gift that families and firms should use. She'd push for apprenticeships to change now so young people are ready.
S4.think: Privately she'd still worry because offices shrink well before 2036. But reaching fifty-three with the house and workshop nearly paid, she'd have time to build the adaptations business slowly.
S4.do: Keeps leading her crew and apprentice scheme for four or five years. Starts the side business with her husband around year three and supports her daughter's plan to study veterinary science.
S4.feel: Gently uneasy, with time to do it right.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade her focus shifts to doing things slowly and protecting jobs through gradual change. She still sees the office market shrinking but believes time spreads the pain. Her apprentices remain the thread through every scenario.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because the offices go first and then the robots come for both of us. What would help is updated apprenticeships run by firms, and help for families that comes with work attached. And time, really, but you can't buy that.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the young ones. Everybody asks people like me, with savings and a house. The nineteen-year-old apprentice with nothing is the one who'll really feel it.

headlineQuote: The nineteen-year-old apprentice with nothing is the one who'll really feel it.
portrait: Chloe Silva is a 43-year-old lead hand on a city-centre fit-out crew, married to a self-employed electrician, with a daughter of thirteen and a son of eight. She runs her firm's apprentice scheme, inspired by a church mentor who gave her a start, and uses AI now and then but checks everything twice. She's calm under the plateau, uneasy under steady change because shrinking offices mean fewer fit-outs, and alarmed by AGI in two years. With more time she'd build a side business adapting homes for older people, testing it carefully before relying on it.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because offices empty first and then robots reach both her and her husband's trades.
whatWouldHelp: Updated apprenticeships run by firms, help for families that comes with work attached, and time to adjust.
